summary: This informational RFC looks at the technical side of blocking and filtering Internet services. It describes common approaches and discusses their effects on the network and on users, including unintended side effects and ways they can be bypassed, to help policy makers and engineers understand the trade-offs.

plainLanguage.summary: Some people want to block parts of the internet. This explains the different ways to do it and why each can break other things or fail to work.

questions: side effects of blocking internet services
subtitle: Technical trade-offs and consequences of blocking and filtering Internet services.

tldr.problem: Governments, enterprises, and network operators want to block or filter Internet services and content they deem undesirable, but different technical approaches have very different consequences for the Internet's architecture and for unrelated services.
tldr.mechanism: This document examines four broad technical approaches—network-based blocking (firewalls, DNS filtering), rendezvous-based blocking (domain seizures, routing controls), endpoint-based blocking (client-side filters, server-side restrictions), and hybrid approaches—evaluating each against criteria like scope, granularity, efficacy, and security impact.
tldr.outcome: Policy makers and engineers can understand what happens when they choose a particular blocking method, including unintended side effects that may harm legitimate services and the limits of effectiveness given Internet resilience.

facts.label: Primary threat to architecture
facts.value: Breaking end-to-end assumptions and trust infrastructures

today: RFC 7754 is an Informational RFC from the Internet Architecture Board that remains relevant to the ongoing debate over content blocking and filtering. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Scope of Blocking and Filtering
sections.content:
Blocking and filtering of Internet services is not new. Firewalls have been part of network security for decades. However, the use of blocking has shifted: from protecting a single organization's network to blocking imposed on users without their knowledge or consent. Governments, enterprises, and ISPs increasingly seek to prevent access to specific content or services—whether for security (malware prevention), policy (restricting access to certain websites), or law enforcement (blocking infringing material).

This RFC is not a judgment on whether filtering is lawful or ethical. Instead, it analyzes the technical mechanisms and their consequences. It helps policy makers and engineers understand what happens when they block: what breaks, what still gets through, and what side effects may harm innocent third parties.

The document distinguishes between blocking (preventing access in aggregate) and filtering (preventing access to specific items within an aggregate). In practice, the distinction does not lead to different conclusions, so the two terms are treated as equivalent.
sections.plainLanguage: Blocking is common—firewalls do it—but this explains what happens technically when you block something and what else might break.

sections.title: Common Blocking and Filtering Methods
sections.content:
Several blocking techniques have emerged:

Firewalls and Packet Filtering: Stateless filters block by rules (e.g., "block all traffic to port 25"). Stateful filters block based on connection state (e.g., "block inbound traffic that is not a response to an outbound request"). Deep packet inspection (DPI) can filter based on content inside the packet.

Web Filtering: HTTPS presents a challenge: the requested URI is encrypted. Filters either block by network address and port (crude, affects many sites on the same IP), or act as a man-in-the-middle by presenting a forged HTTPS certificate.

Spam Filtering: Email filters use lists of known spam sources, content-based heuristics, and signature verification. Filters can run on the user's device, the mail server, or a third-party MX proxy.

Domain Name Seizure: Authorities can prevent domain name resolution by modifying DNS responses, redirecting to a seizure notice page, or seizing the domain at the registrar. This blocks all services under that domain globally, even outside the enforcing jurisdiction.

DNS Manipulation: Intermediate resolvers can return incorrect answers for domains, intercepting requests. This contradicts DNS security assumptions and can break DNSSEC validation.

Routing and Addressing Control: Governments have frozen address allocations and manipulated routing to control access. These attacks harm the global address and routing systems.

Safe Browsing: Web browsers check URLs against lists of malicious sites before loading them. This is typically on the client side and is transparent to servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Blocking happens at many levels: routers (firewalls), DNS servers, browsers, mail systems, and address registries. Each level has different reach and costs.

sections.title: Evaluating Blocking Approaches
sections.content:
The document proposes four criteria for evaluating any blocking approach:

Scope: How many hosts and users are affected? Blocking at a network boundary affects all users on that network. Blocking at an endpoint affects only that device. Different jurisdictions have different scope.

Granularity: Can the blocker target specific content, or does it have to block an entire service? A firewall blocking port 80 blocks all HTTP traffic. A proxy filtering HTTP requests can target specific URIs. Coarse-grained blocking causes collateral damage to legitimate services on the same infrastructure.

Efficacy: How easy is it to bypass? Blocking by IP address fails if services move or use shared hosting. Blocking by domain name fails if the service uses a new domain. Encryption and distributed systems make blocking harder.

Security: Does the blocking undermine existing security infrastructure? Man-in-the-middle HTTPS inspection breaks certificate pinning. DNS manipulation breaks DNSSEC. Manipulating routing breaks path integrity. These side effects harm security far beyond the blocked service.
sections.plainLanguage: Blocking is not simple: it might affect the wrong people, might break other things, might not actually work, and might weaken security for everyone.

sections.title: Four Approaches to Blocking and Their Trade-offs
sections.content:
Network-Based Blocking: Firewalls and ISP filters operate at network boundaries or intermediate routers. They have broad scope (affecting all users on the network) but coarse granularity (hard to target specific content without blocking legitimate uses). Efficacy is moderate—services can migrate IP addresses or hide traffic in encryption. Security impact is high if the blocking mechanism compromises trust (e.g., HTTPS inspection) or if it interferes with legitimate security protocols.

Rendezvous-Based Blocking: Domain seizures and DNS redirection block at the "rendezvous point" where users learn how to reach a service. These have lower scope (only affecting users of that specific DNS resolver or those subject to court jurisdiction) but fine granularity (targeting a specific domain). Efficacy is variable: users can switch DNS resolvers, or the service can obtain a new domain name. Security impact is severe—DNS manipulation contradicts DNSSEC assumptions and can cause widespread validation failures.

Endpoint-Based Blocking: Client-side filters (browser extensions, parental controls) or server-side restrictions (refusing service to certain clients) affect only the endpoints involved. Scope is narrow, granularity can be very fine (targeting a specific resource), and security impact is minimal because the user controls their own endpoint. However, efficacy is poor—determined users can disable or circumvent client-side controls, and servers may refuse to restrict service without legal compulsion.

Hybrid Approaches: Combining multiple methods (network + DNS + client-side) increases coverage but also multiplies side effects and costs.
sections.plainLanguage: Network blocking is fast but crude and breaks other things. DNS blocking is fine-grained but users can work around it. Client-side blocking is safe but only works for one person. Each approach has trade-offs.

sections.title: Implications for Internet Architecture
sections.content:
The RFC's key insight is that blocking and filtering are architectural choices with consequences. The original Internet design assumed end-to-end control: endpoints are trusted, and the network is neutral. Blocking often breaks this assumption.

When possible, the best approach from an architecture perspective is endpoint-based blocking with transparency: inform endpoints about potentially undesirable services, and let the communicants decide whether to engage. This respects user autonomy, has minimal collateral damage, and strengthens rather than weakens security.

However, the document acknowledges that some parties will choose network-based or rendezvous-based blocking anyway, for policy or enforcement reasons. In those cases, the consequences include:

  • Collateral damage: Blocking one service often blocks others (shared hosting, shared infrastructure). Many services on a single IP address, or DNS zone, suffer when one is blocked.
  • Limited efficacy: Determined actors can circumvent most blocking by moving, re-naming, using encryption, or tunneling.
  • Security side effects: Man-in-the-middle interception, DNS manipulation, routing control, and other blocking mechanisms undermine trust infrastructures that protect legitimate services. The cost to everyone's security can exceed the benefit of blocking one bad actor.

These observations are not arguments for or against blocking per se, but rather invitations for blockers to understand the full cost of their approach and to consider less damaging alternatives.
sections.plainLanguage: The safer approach is to tell the user what's risky and let them decide. If you block it anyway, you'll probably break other things, it won't fully work, and it might hurt everyone's security.
